What makes volcanoes and earthquakes so amazing?

Volcanoes and earthquakes, when the ground shakes and mountains spew fire, show us that the Earth is alive. They're scary, but they're also truly fascinating natural events.

content.alt: Volcanoes and earthquakes - Nature and science facts about volcanoes and earthquakes
content.text:
Nature and science facts about volcanoes and earthquakes

The Earth's outer shell (the crust) is divided into giant pieces called tectonic plates that move a few centimeters each year. When plates collide or slide past each other and the ground shakes, that's an earthquake. Melted rock deep underground is called magma, and when a volcano erupts and it comes out, we call it lava (about 700 to 1,200°C). Once lava cools, it becomes solid rock (like basalt).

Great points to explore together

Point out things like tectonic plates (movement), magma vs. lava (the difference), volcanoes (eruptions), and earthquakes (shaking). Talking together about "Why is it so hot deep inside the Earth?" is a wonderful way to explore.

content.alt: Volcanoes and earthquakes - Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Try a "volcano eruption experiment" with baking soda and vinegar (foam bursts out). Wobble some pudding or jelly to compare it to the shaking of an earthquake, and it's a great time to practice earthquake safety together (protect your head, get under a table).

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What's the difference between magma and lava?
A. When it's deep underground it's called magma, and when a volcano erupts and it comes out, it's called lava. They're the same melted rock.

Q. Why do earthquakes happen?
A. Because when giant tectonic plates collide or slide past each other, that force shakes the ground.

Q. How can we explore this at home?
A. Try a baking soda and vinegar volcano experiment, and practice earthquake safety (protect your head, get under a table).
